source_terms: it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer
item.claim: Bijapurkar identifies a specific misdiagnosis and corrects it. When richer consumers began buying popular-segment rather than premium products, marketers called this "down-trading" and "many have suggested that this is the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy." Her correction: "In fact, it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer and the popular and discount segments, in many cases, now offer a real value advantage in terms of equivalent if not better benefits at a lower price." She supplies the supply-side cause: unequal tax and duty incentives were withdrawn, forcing small manufacturers into open competition, which produced "rogue" marketers who refused to respect the unwritten price-performance rules, so consumers faced an explosion of new price-performance combinations. She gives the automotive instances — a 125cc motorcycle at a 100cc popular price, premium styling at discount prices, a B- segment car with premium features — and concludes that "the paradigm of premium-popular-discount = rich-middle income-poor is now quite irrelevant."

mechanism.text: Observed behaviour changed because the choice set changed, not because preferences did. When the price-performance frontier moves, a buyer whose preferences are unchanged will appear at a different point on the old segmentation — and an analyst who holds the segmentation fixed will attribute the movement to the buyer's character.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets after the withdrawal of differential tax and duty structures, principally FMCG, automotive, PCs and industrial water treatment, over roughly 1991-2009.

caveats.text: THE GENERAL SHAPE IS THE VALUABLE PART AND IT IS NOT INDIAN. Attributing a shift in observed behaviour to consumer character when the choice set moved is a reasoning error available anywhere. The specific instances are dated
the cases are named products and are checkable in principle, but no market-share, price or volume data is given for any of them

the author also offers a second, different explanation elsewhere for the same FMCG stagnation — a 'change confluence' in which consumer credit and durables purchases committed future income, forcing careful FMCG spending. The two explanations are compatible but are not reconciled, and the book presents each as sufficient in its own place

INSPECTED: Figure 4.2, the premium-popular-discount construct, was opened. It is a schematic price-against-performance diagram showing the traditional line and three 'new offering' positions below it; it carries no data and is an illustration of the argument, not evidence for it

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: Named cases without figures; a competing explanation for the same phenomenon appears elsewhere in the book unreconciled.

source_stated_problems: a shift in observed behaviour caused by a moving choice set is attributed to consumer character
source_stated_remedies: check whether the price-performance frontier moved before attributing a behaviour change to the buyer

Maruti Swift, a 'B' segment car with premium-category features

item.question: What study are the 30% and 17% figures attributed to, and which of the three pages tells you the sample size?
item.answer: All three attribute them to a Google/Kantar study called "The Short & the Long of ABCDs Effectiveness", global, dated April 2021 — but only the Google for Business resources article gives a sample, "n=11,000 ads". Google Ads Help cites the same study, publisher, scope and month with no sample size. Think with Google cites it as "Google/Kantar Link AI, Global, The Short and the Long of ABCDs Effectiveness, 2021", naming Kantar's Link AI, dropping the month and giving no sample size. The study itself is not linked or published on any of the pages.
item.support: The three footnotes differ as described. n=11,000 ads appears only in the resources article's footnote.
confounders: attributing the sample size to the Google Ads Help page, which is the page most often cited but does not give it
assuming n=11,000 refers to people surveyed rather than ads
conflating this Kantar study with the separate Ipsos collaboration described on Think with Google, which has no stated sample

item.question: Marketers observed richer consumers buying popular-segment products and called it down-trading. What does this source say was actually happening, and what is the general shape of the error?
item.answer: That the direction of the inference was wrong. The observation was read as a consumer trait — 'many have suggested that this is the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy' — and her correction is that 'it is not the consumer who has "down-traded" but the supplier who has "up-traded" his offer', so the popular and discount segments in many cases now offered equivalent or better benefits at a lower price. She supplies the supply-side cause: unequal tax and duty incentives were withdrawn, forcing small manufacturers into open competition, which produced 'rogue' marketers who refused to respect the unwritten price-performance rules, so consumers faced an explosion of new price-performance combinations. Her instances are automotive — a 125cc motorcycle at a 100cc popular price, premium styling at discount prices, a B-segment car with premium features — and her conclusion is that 'the paradigm of premium-popular-discount = rich-middle income-poor is now quite irrelevant'. THE GENERAL SHAPE is attributing a change in observed behaviour to a change in the people, when what changed was the set of options they faced. Figure 4.2 was opened in this pass and carries no data: it is a price-against-performance schematic, so it illustrates the argument and is not evidence for it. No switching data is supplied anywhere.
item.support: 'it is not the consumer who has "down-traded" but the supplier who has "up-traded" his offer'
item.confounders: Character explanations are attractive because they need no data and predict everything. This is the book's clearest instance, and its correction is also unmeasured.

item.question: This source denies that film clothing reflects real clothing while also insisting the audience brings a real-world grammar to it. How do both hold at once?
item.answer: They hold at different levels. The denial is about correspondence: 'the relationship between women's clothes in movies and in real life is not one of reflection, but the codes of cinema require clothing to fill particular semiotic functions'. The insistence is about legibility: the audience brings a widely understood grammar of wearing the sari, with occasions requiring different saris by season, time of day and degree of formality, plus a colour code — red, green and yellow for festive occasions, white or pale for widows, black largely a Western fashion. The cinematic code is built ON that grammar without copying it. So the heroine almost invariably wore a sari as an emblem of chastity in contrast with the vamp, the unmarried heroine wears Western clothes before marriage and changes into salwar-khamees or a sari after it, and mothers and mother-figures always wear a sari. Real dress supplies the vocabulary; the films use it to mark moral and narrative position, not to record what people wore.
item.support: 'the relationship between women's clothes in movies and in real life is not one of reflection, but the codes of cinema require clothing to fill particular semiotic functions'
item.confounders: Both halves are routinely dropped. Reading film dress as documentary evidence of period dress ignores the first; reading it as arbitrary costume design ignores the second.

source_terms: the sari is heavily laden with cultural meanings of nostalgia, tradition, womanhood, nationalism and social status
a widely understood grammar of wearing the sari exists
item.claim: Dwyer states that "the relationship between women's clothes in movies and in real life is not one of reflection, but the codes of cinema require clothing to fill particular semiotic functions," and then traces those functions. She reports a real-world grammar that the audience brings: a widely understood grammar of wearing the sari, with specific occasions requiring different saris by season, time of day and degree of formality, and a colour code (red, green and yellow for festive occasions; white or pale for widows; black largely a Western fashion). She then reports the cinematic use built on it — in older films contrasting the heroine with the vamp, the heroine almost invariably wore a sari as an emblem of chastity and goodness; the unmarried heroine wears Western clothes before marriage and changes into salwar-khamees or a sari after it; mothers and mother-figures always wear traditional sober saris.

mechanism.text: The garment carries meaning before it reaches the film, so the film does not have to construct the meaning; it selects from a code the viewer already holds. This is why costume can mark marital status, age, class, region, religion and moral position without dialogue, and why the same garment changes what it says when worn by a different character type.

scope.conditions: Stated for Hindi cinema and for the Indian dress conventions of the period the book covers, with the sari's own standardisation described as recent ("the sari is seen as the national dress of Indian women, but this is only a recent fashion"). Dwyer explicitly dates changes: the heroine of the 1990s can wear Western clothes with no negative implication, which she says was not earlier the case.

caveats.text: the source dates the code's own change inside the book — Western clothes on the heroine carried a moral charge earlier and did not by the 1990s. The grammar is not stable and the source says so
'almost invariably', 'always', 'often' are the quantifiers used throughout; no counts over any corpus are given anywhere in the costume section

the code is described for one audience. Nothing in the source supports its transfer to viewers who do not hold it, and the book's own Conclusion reports that films are 'finding it hard to reach out beyond the South Asian diasporic audience'

Adjacency to sk_dpci_0120 recorded without a graph edge: the same code is read off posters, where it does more work. The original extraction used a 'supports' relation, which SPEC-03 does not define; no permitted relation expresses it from this object's side, so it is kept as an observation rather than expressed as a fabricated edge.

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: Rich and specific, but entirely unquantified: the pattern is asserted over an unnamed corpus.
